claim: Aristotelian practical judgment is compared with political ends; no claim of an unbroken institutional tradition.
Plato’s concern with stable objects of knowledge returns in his own argument about who should rule; not Plato learning from Aristotle.
Greek participation and Roman legal status differ; neither is modern equal personhood.
Two different purposes of textual editing, not a claimed direct Alexandrian institutional descent.
The Justinianic compilation circulated and was glossed in medieval Latin legal scholarship; Arabic philosophy has its own, separately retained route.
A return to what rule is for, not a claim that Hobbes simply continues Aristotle.
Common humanity is compared with consenting political membership, not identified with it.
An alternative comparison reaches the same rights question, without asserting Locke as the sole source of rights declarations.
The claim is tested against revolutionary agency and changing law; no monocausal European intellectual origin.
A later archive comparison, not an asserted direct influence on the Haitian constitution.
A historical contradiction motivates a design question, not a guarantee that the future institution succeeds.
